title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks - Standards & Guidance
author: Ari Chen
content:
Summary:
This page defines Redwood Inference's standards and operational guidance for SRE-owned Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning practices, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling expectations, and canonical runbooks. Guidance below standardizes how teams define, measure, and act on reliability goals across Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Scope:
- Applies to all externally-facing inference endpoints and internal critical services (control plane, scheduler, routing).
- Non-critical helper services should adopt a simplified SLO (see 'Non-critical services' below).

Goals:
- Provide a consistent approach for SLO design and error budget consumption/guardrails.
- Ensure capacity planning ties SLOs to predictable infrastructure and on-call actions.
- Standardize incident reviews and reliability initiative workflows to reduce recurrence.
- Define minimum tooling and dashboards required for operational readiness.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets
Overview:
- Every service must have at least one availability SLO and one latency SLO where relevant. SLOs are defined at the logical user-visible surface (e.g., /v1/generate, embeddings API) rather than individual microservices.
- SLO window: default is 30-day rolling window. 90-day windows can be used for long-lived products after approval from Eng-SRE.
- SLI sources: Prometheus metrics (service:request_success_count{...}, service:request_total_count{...}), distributed tracing latency histograms (p50/p95/p99), and synthetic checks (external health checks).

SLO standard table (required fields):
- SLO name | SLI | Target | Window | Error budget | Owner (team) | Alerting threshold | Notes
- Hosted API - availability | successful_responses / total_requests | 99.95% | 30d | 0.05% | eng-api | error budget burn > 2x in 24h | primary customer-facing SLO
- Hosted API - latency (generate p95) | request_duration_ms p95 | < 450ms | 30d | N/A (objective) | eng-api | p95 > 600ms for 1h | for interactive workloads
- Model-serving - tail latency p99 | kv_cache_hit_request_duration_ms p99 | < 1500ms | 30d | N/A | serving-runtime | p99 > 2000ms for 15m | applies to Dedicated GPUs
- Control plane - availability | controlplane_success_count / controlplane_total | 99.9% | 30d | 0.1% | eng-platform | error budget burn > 1.5x in 24h | impacts private deployments provisioning

Error budget policy (standard):
1. Error budget is computed as (1 - target) * window. Teams must publish a daily error budget burn rate chart to the SLO dashboard.
2. If burn rate > 2x expected over 24h: on-call must open a reliability ticket, notify the owner team, and run mitigations (see runbooks).
3. If burn rate > 4x expected over 6h or remaining budget < 25%: impose a soft freeze on non-essential deploys (team CI/CD gate) until postmortem/mitigation plan approved by SRE.
4. If budget exhausted: immediate change freeze and executive notification; SRE and team must run emergency remediation and schedule a post-incident review within 72 hours.

2) Capacity Planning
Principles:
- Capacity planning ties demand SLOs (throughput/latency) to fleet sizing, autoscaling policies, and reserve headroom.
- Plan for N+25% headroom at expected peak per region for Hosted API; Dedicated capacity SLAs use contract-specified headroom.

Required artifacts for every service (capacity playbook):
- Current steady-state QPS and 95th percentile request size (tokens or bytes).
- Traffic growth assumptions (3, 6, 12 months).
- Tail-latency sensitivity to queue depth and batch size (benchmarks).
- Autoscaler config (min/max replicas, target CPU/GPU utilization, queue length thresholds).
- Cost vs latency trade-off analysis (recommended quantization/batching knobs).

Capacity planning procedure (quarterly):
1. Gather metrics (QPS by route, batch size distribution, avg tokens) for the last 90 days.
2. Run capacity simulation using the performance bench (see eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite).
3. Identify bottlenecks (GPU saturation, network egress, scheduler queueing) and create mitigation items.
4. Update Infra Terraform (capacity commit) with at least two weeks lead time for major GPU purchases or cloud reservations.
5. Validate with canary traffic for 48 hours before ramp.

Sizing heuristics (example):
- For a 70B encoder-decoder model: baseline throughput per A100-80GB ~ 6 tokens/sec single request stream; plan for batching improvements.
- Use 95th percentile tokens-per-request to compute per-GPU concurrency planning.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Roadmap
- All owner teams must maintain a quarterly Reliability Initiative (RI) list that maps to SLO weaknesses identified from incident reviews and error budget trends.
- Typical RIs: prefix KV-cache, batching improvements, model quantization to reduce memory footprint, autoscaler tuning, enhanced synthetic checks.
- Each RI should include: success criteria (SLO delta or cost reduction), owner, timeline, required infra changes, and rollback plan.

4) Incident Review Standards
Mandatory post-incident items for Sev2+ incidents affecting SLOs:
- TL;DR summary (1-3 sentences)
- Timeline with timestamps (iso8601) and owner annotations
- Root cause analysis (RCA) with evidence (logs, traces, screenshots)
- What went well / what went poorly
- Action items with owner and due date (no anonymous tasks)
- Error budget impact calculation and follow-up actions (deployment freeze, RI creation)
- Executive summary for incidents that cross 1% of monthly error budget

Post-incident timeline expectations:
- Initial incident review draft within 72 hours of mitigation/completion.
- Finalized postmortem and at least one follow-up action completed within 30 days.

5) Operational Tooling and Dashboards
Minimum dashboard and alert requirements per SLO:
- SLO dashboard: rolling-window SLO graph (30d), daily burn rate, remaining budget percentage, top contributing error sources (by tag).
- Synthetic monitors: global external checks every 5m for primary routes from at least 3 regions.
- Heatmap: latency by region and model variant (p50/p95/p99).
- Capacity dashboard: GPU utilization (p50/p95), queue depth, batch size distribution, autoscaler events.

Alerting guidance (example Prometheus rules):
- slo_error_budget_burn_rate > 2 for 1h -> severity P2 notify on-call + owner team Slack channel
- p95_request_latency_seconds > 1.5x target for 15m -> P2 alert to on-call
- gpu_utilization > 92% for 30m -> P1 paging alert to infra on-call
- synthetic_check_failure_rate > 3% for 15m -> P1 paging

Suggested alert destinations:
- PagerDuty for P1/P0 paging alerts
- Slack + Ops channel for P2/P3
- Jira reliability tickets for any error budget mitigation requiring >8h of work

6) Canonical Runbooks (examples)
A. High availability degradation - Hosted API availability SLO breach
Steps:
1. Triage: confirm SLI source and scope (prometheus query + synthetic checks).
   - promql: sum(rate(service_request_failed_total[5m])) / sum(rate(service_request_total[5m]))
2. Scope: identify affected routes, regions, and model variants.
3. Mitigate: rotate traffic to healthy region or compatible model variant via routing policy:
   - CLI: rictl route set-weight --route /v1/generate --region us-west-2 --weight 0
4. If degradation due to capacity: scale up reserved pool or add burst capacity (Dedicated) or increase autoscaler max (Hosted).
5. Notify: notify pg-reliability Slack channel and the customer-impact channel.
6. Execute post-incident tasks and update SLO dashboard.

B. Tail latency spike - model serving p99 breach
Steps:
1. Identify whether KV cache hit rate dropped: query: rate(kv_cache_hit_total[5m]) / rate(kv_cache_lookup_total[5m])
2. If cache miss storm: invalidate troublesome cache keys and re-populate with warm-up synthetic requests.
3. Reduce batch size or temporarily lower concurrency to shed queueing: update batcher config and restart worker set if required.
4. If a new model variant introduced regression: rollback model version in the deployment config and re-route traffic.

C. Control plane provisioning failures
Steps:
1. Check control plane health endpoint and DB connectivity.
2. If DB latency high, fail fast provisioning and surface a clear 503 to customer with ETA.
3. Engage eng-platform and follow control-plane runbook to restart api-workers and failover DB read-replicas.

Runbook quality checklist (before marking complete):
- Clear owner and escalation path (name and PagerDuty role)
- Exact commands / dashboards / queries included
- Rollback and mitigation steps defined
- Test procedure for runbook (game-day or tabletop)
- Last-tested date noted in runbook header

7) Roles & Responsibilities
- Owner team: defines SLO, maintains runbooks, executes capacity planning and RIs.
- Eng-SRE: reviews SLO definitions, enforces error budget policy, manages synthetic monitoring and alerting templates, conducts quarterly reliability audits.
- Eng-Platform / Infra: provides capacity allocation, autoscaler primitives, and tooling to implement freezes/CI gates.
- Product: supports rollout decisions and customer communication when SLOs are materially impacted.

8) Exceptions and governance
- Any deviation from the standards (SLO window, error budget policy, or alert thresholds) requires an ADR and Eng-SRE approval.
- Reduced SLO targets for non-customer-facing internal tooling must be documented and approved by Eng-SRE.

Appendices
A. Useful PromQL snippets
- Availability SLI: 1 - (sum(rate(service_request_failed_total[5m])) / sum(rate(service_request_total[5m])))
- Error budget burn rate (24h): (1 - SLO_target) / (remaining_error_budget / projected_24h_errors) - implement via recorded rules combining SLO window summaries.

B. Postmortem template (copy into new incident ticket):
- Title:
- Severity:
- Start/End (iso8601):
- Impact summary:
- Timeline:
- Root cause:
- Mitigations taken:
- Action items (owner, due date):
- Error budget impact:
- Lessons learned:
